entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Gaius Licinius Stolo (c. 450 - 400 BCE) was a Roman tribune who played a pivotal role in the plebeian reforms of ancient Rome.

He was one of the two tribunes who opened the consulship to the plebeians, a measure that had significant consequences for the social and political fabric of Rome.

This reform, known as the 'Second Plebeian Secession', was a major turning point in the struggle for power between the patrician class and the common people.

The plebeians, who had previously been excluded from the highest offices of state, were now able to elect their own magistrates, leading to a significant shift in the balance of power in Rome.

This event marked the beginning of a new era in Roman history, one in which the plebeians would increasingly play a major role in shaping the course of the city's development.

The legacy of Stolo's reforms can still be seen today in the enduring influence of the Roman Republic on modern Western politics.

'When the plebeians have the right to elect their magistrates, the Republic is secure.' - Gaius Licinius Stolo
